summary: Lists the situations where DNS, protected by DNSSEC, could help a client decide whether a TLS server is really the one it claims to be. Today that job is mostly done by certificate authorities, and the DNS could add extra assertions. This informational document gathers the use cases and requirements that led to the DANE work.

plainLanguage.summary: When you visit a website, your computer wants proof it is the right one. Right now it asks trusted certificate-givers. This note imagines also checking the internet's phone book, so there is a second way to confirm.

questions: use dnssec to authenticate tls servers
why use dnssec for tls authentication
subtitle: The scenarios and requirements for letting DNSSEC-signed DNS back up the certificates that TLS clients check.

tldr.problem: TLS clients trust certificate authorities to bind domain names to public keys, and a mis-issued certificate from any widely used CA can let an attacker pose as a service.
tldr.mechanism: With DNSSEC, a domain holder can publish signed DNS information about its certificates or CAs. The RFC lists four use cases and a set of requirements for a mechanism that does this.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational requirements document, not a protocol. It sets the goals that the DANE mechanism was meant to meet.

today: RFC 6394 is an Informational document and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It records the use cases and requirements for DANE rather than specifying a protocol.

sections.title: The Problem With Today's TLS Trust
sections.content:
Many protocols use TLS to protect client-server connections. A client finds a server by its DNS name, runs a TLS handshake, and receives a PKIX certificate. The client validates that the certificate chains to one of its trust anchors, then checks that the name in it matches the domain it wanted.

The weak point is that clients rely on certificate authorities (CAs) to bind keys to domain names correctly. An attacker who obtains a mis-issued certificate from one widely used CA can authenticate as the victim's domain. If the attacker can also sit in the middle, for example through DNS cache poisoning of an A or AAAA record, the client is fooled.

With DNSSEC, clients can verify that DNS data came from the domain operator and was not tampered with. DANE (DNS-based Authentication of Named Entities) aims to use that to add assurance to the TLS handshake. The RFC says it applies to any application using TLS with a domain-named service, even though it often uses HTTPS as its example.
sections.plainLanguage: Right now your computer trusts a few big certificate-givers to say who is who. If one of them makes a fake ID, a trickster can pretend to be a website. DANE is the idea of also checking a second, signed list.

sections.title: Definitions and Cast of Characters
sections.content:
The RFC reuses standard PKIX, DNSSEC and TLS terms. Here server means the server role in TLS, not a host, since several servers can share one host on different ports with different certificates.

A domain holder is the entity authorized to control the contents of a zone, such as the registrant of a 2nd- or 3rd-level domain. The holder is not necessarily the entity that operates the zone. A valid DNSSEC signature does not by itself mean the domain holder authorized the signed records.

The use cases follow a cast: Alice runs the service at alice.example.com and its zone, Bob is a client, Charlie is a well-known CA, Oscar is an outsourcing provider, and Trent is a CA that is not well known.
sections.plainLanguage: The note tells its stories with named people: Alice owns a website, Bob visits it, and others play the certificate-givers and helpers. It also separates the owner of a name from whoever runs the phone book entry.

sections.title: CA and Certificate Constraints
sections.content:
In the CA constraints case, Alice has a certificate from Charlie and fears other well-known CAs could issue one for her name without permission. She wants visitors to expect a certificate issued under Charlie and no other CA. Bob checks that, and still does normal PKIX validation to a trust anchor. Alice could publish the same hint for CAs, so Charlie can check whether Alice authorized him before issuing.

In the service certificate constraints case, Alice goes further and tells Bob that one specific certificate must be the first in the server Certificate message's certificate_list. The security analysis matches the CA case.

For both, the RFC says DANE data could in principle be used without DNSSEC, but that adds only a very small incremental benefit. Because PKIX validation is still required, falsified records cannot let someone masquerade as the server without also getting a certificate, so the worst case is today's level of risk. False records could be used for denial of service, but an attacker who can alter DNS responses already has simpler ways to do that.
sections.plainLanguage: Alice can say: only this certificate-giver, or even only this exact ID card, is allowed for my website. Bob still does his normal checks too, so a fake note in the phone book cannot help a trickster by itself.

sections.title: Domain-Issued Certificates and Trust Anchors
sections.content:
Alice may want to issue her own certificates without any external CA. A self-signed certificate alone does not help Bob, because he does not hold Alice's trust anchor and cannot tell it from an attacker's. So Alice publishes information that lets Bob treat her CA as a trust anchor for alice.example.com. Using Trent's lesser-known CA is functionally the same, with Bob learning Trent's trust anchor through DANE. Bob may still refuse it under local policy.

This case clearly requires DNSSEC, since injected or corrupted records could make clients trust an attacker's certificate. Deleted records cause connection failure, which could push clients to reconnect without TLS (a downgrade attack). So applications must forbid falling back to unsecured channels when records appear deleted, for example when a missing record has no NSEC or NSEC3 record.

It also gives the most power to DNS operators, who control a zone's contents and signing. That matters when the operator differs from the domain holder, as in DNS hosting. The RFC notes DNS operators can already obtain certificates from some well-known CAs today by manipulating the values CAs use to verify domain control.
sections.plainLanguage: Alice might hand out her own ID cards instead of asking a big certificate-giver. Bob can only trust them if the signed phone book vouches for her. The person who keeps the phone book has a lot of power, so that matters.

sections.title: Delegated Services and Other Requirements
sections.content:
When Oscar operates the service for Alice, three DNS setups are possible. In the first, Alice keeps the A/AAAA records and signs them with the DANE record, which needs tight coordination with Oscar. In the second, she delegates a sub-domain to Oscar and controls nothing under it. In the third, Alice holds the DANE records and delegates only address records to Oscar's DNS server, so Oscar can move servers freely.

Where Alice controls the DANE records she can constrain which certificates Oscar presents, but must update the records when Oscar changes certificates. Where Oscar controls them he is more autonomous, and Alice cannot enforce anything.

Section 4 lists operational requirements: Multiple Ports, No Downgrade, Encapsulation, Predictability, Opportunistic Security, Combination, Roll-over, Simple Key Management, Minimal Dependencies, Minimal Options, Wildcards and Redirection (CNAME or DNAME chains). Clients that do not support DANE must keep working as specified whether or not DANE data is present.
sections.plainLanguage: If a helper runs the website for Alice, the DNS entries can be kept by Alice, by the helper, or split. Who holds them decides who is in control. The note also lists rules for the final design, such as being simple and not letting a trickster switch security off.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's security section is brief. The general effect of DANE-style mechanisms is to increase the role of DNS operators in authentication, either in place of or in addition to third-party actors such as commercial CAs. The specific implications are discussed in each use case above.
sections.plainLanguage: Using the internet's phone book to prove who is who means the people who run the phone book matter more, and the big certificate-givers matter a little less.
